passage: I sit behind Nikita in maths, so I notice things. Every time Mrs. Rao passes our row, she stops at Dev's and Anya's desks and says, "Lovely work." Nikita's hand goes up for questions and sometimes gets skipped. Yesterday she wrote a long answer and looked around after, but the teacher did not check her page. Nikita put her head down for a bit. I don't know whether the teacher meant it or just did not see. Today Nikita went to the front after class and asked for help with a sum, and Mrs. Rao sat down with her. I am Gautam.

qa.q: Which two children does Mrs. Rao praise at their desks?
qa.a: She stops at Dev's and Anya's desks and says, "Lovely work."

qa.q: What might Nikita have been feeling when she put her head down?
qa.a: She may have felt overlooked and a little sad, though Gautam cannot be sure whether that is what she felt.

qa.q: What could Nikita do if she still feels unseen by her teacher?
qa.a: She can keep doing her best, keep asking for help as she did, and talk to her teacher or a parent if it still seems unfair.

qa.q: How might Mrs. Rao explain her behaviour if asked?
qa.a: She may not have noticed she was giving some children more attention, or she may have simply been busy; it might be real or not.

grounding: A classmate observes a child who feels invisible next to teacher favourites, who asks for help; it may or may not be real favouritism.

passage: 'Thomas, you think your teacher only sees the clever ones? Let me tell you about myself. I'm Hansa Aunty now, but at ten I was the invisible girl at the back. Our teacher always picked the same three girls to read aloud, to carry the register, to lead prayer. I felt like a chair. I sulked for weeks and stopped doing my homework neatly. Then my mother said, "Ask her for something." So I stayed back and asked Madam to help me with long division. She looked at me properly for the first time. "You're Hansa, aren't you? Come early tomorrow." Maybe she had favourites. Maybe she just hadn't noticed a quiet girl. But after that, she did notice me.'

qa.q: What did young Hansa ask the teacher to help with?
How did young Hansa feel at the back of the class?
qa.a: Invisible and left out, like a chair, while the same three girls were always picked.

qa.q: What choice in the story changed things for Hansa?
qa.a: Stopping the sulking and staying back to ask the teacher for help.

qa.q: How might the teacher have seen young Hansa before she asked?
qa.a: Perhaps hardly at all; she may simply not have noticed a quiet girl, rather than disliking her.

grounding: An aunt recalls feeling invisible to a teacher with favourites, and how asking for help changed things.

passage: With only one day left before annual day, Nirmala Ma'am handed out the last speaking parts, again to the same four girls who always sat in front. Bidisha, who had practised the narrator's lines for weeks, was put in the chorus at the back. She felt invisible. Rain hammered the hall's tin roof, and the rehearsal kept stopping for leaks. During a break, Bidisha almost went to sulk in the corner. Instead she walked up. 'Ma'am, I know all the narrator's lines. Could I be the understudy? And can you tell me what I need to work on?' Nirmala Ma'am blinked. 'I didn't know you'd learnt them. Say the first part.' Bidisha did, over the rain. Ma'am nodded slowly. 'Understudy. And speak louder. You have a good voice.'

qa.q: Where was Bidisha put for annual day?
qa.a: In the chorus at the back.

qa.q: How did Bidisha feel when the parts went to the same four girls?
qa.a: Invisible and hurt, after practising the narrator's lines for weeks.

qa.q: What did Bidisha do instead of sulking?
qa.a: She asked to be the understudy and asked what she needed to work on.

qa.q: Why might Nirmala Ma'am have overlooked Bidisha?
qa.a: She didn't know Bidisha had learnt the lines, so it may have been not noticing rather than unfairness.

grounding: A day before annual day a girl who feels overlooked by a teacher speaks up and asks for help instead of sulking.
